sources.locator: Delegates in Tucumán declared independence of the United Provinces in 1816 after the 1810 revolution. Original Spanish preamble, 1853 constitution with 1994 amendments and continuing federal republican framework. The so-called Conquest of the Desert was a violent culmination of long relations among Indigenous peoples, settlers and the Argentine state, not conquest of empty land. State-approved military campaigns across Patagonia 1878–85, including 1879 Río Negro expedition. 1884 law established common, free, compulsory, gradual primary education. Tango developed among urban lower classes in Buenos Aires and Montevideo through European, African-descended and criollo cultural exchange. Yerba mate has Guaraní roots; people share a gourd and bombilla in rounds, with one person preparing and serving, though customs vary. Archive preserves evidence of human-rights crimes in 1976–83 military dictatorship and reparations. 1983 election restored democratic civilian government after the 1976 military dictatorship.

Thirty exact observed intervals, thirty border files, missing summary and card, and initially unreviewed identity, chronology and borders. Exact twenty-five-part geometry, bounds, checksum and tested island and mainland point owners for 1500 to 1000 BCE. Documents the sharp reduction to four components and seams with Ciboney and Arawaks atlas labels. Documents the three-part geometry and seams with Taíno and Arawaks atlas labels. Contains two separate exact-id Polygon features, including Paria and an Amazon-mouth component, beside Taíno and Kalinago labels. Retains only the small mainland component while named Indigenous island layers occupy tested island points. Restores three target components including Barbados and Paria in an editorial reversal after the 1492 snapshot. Reduces the target to two mainland components while colonial and named Indigenous labels own tested island and Paria points. Retains one small Amazon-mouth Polygon through the final exact interval with increased map precision. Confirms exact-id disappearance at the indexed endpoint while peoples, communities and colonial struggles continue.

Original ANU thesis directly read. Printed pp47-56 examine the 1780s-1830s Gia Dinh regime, Minh Huong networks, rice, military supply, 1802 victory, southern autonomy and Minh Mang centralization. Printed pp62-64 reconstruct an early nineteenth-century market, houses, well, festivals, goods and An Thong Canal from named contemporary accounts, while warning that victorious court histories obscure alternatives.

National museum overview checked. It dates the dynasty from 1802, distinguishes its independent and colonial periods, and identifies administrative reform, land development, dikes, flood protection, irrigation and north-south integration. Object listings include nineteenth-century ceramics, furniture, incense burners, writing tools, weights and measures; they are national, not delta-specific samples.

Scholarly book record and indexed contents checked. The work centers southern Vietnam in 1820-1841, identifies Gia Dinh as the regional name after 1802, and treats the 1832 reform as the point when the central court imposed direct rule. Used only for that administrative tension, not details hidden behind the preview.

University history article directly read, especially paragraphs listing the October 1832 dissolution of Gia Dinh Thanh and creation of Phien An, Bien Hoa, Vinh Long, Dinh Tuong, An Giang and Ha Tien provinces, plus the new provincial fiscal, judicial, civil and military offices. The court edict is treated as a government viewpoint.

French national military museum exhibition text checked critically. It traces rivalry, commercial ambitions and religious tensions behind intervention, and the naval conquest of southern Vietnam from 1858 to 1867. Its imperial framing is not adopted and conquest is not described as peaceful modernization. Institutional scholarly essay directly read. It notes the unimplemented 1787 treaty involving future Gia Long, the 1858-1867 conquest of Cochinchina, later expansion into Annam and Tonkin and the 1887 Indochinese Union. Used as a broad chronology with explicit colonial context.

Cambridge chapter abstract checked. It dates the decision and expedition to 1857-1862, the Treaty of Saigon cession to 1862, failed Vietnamese negotiations for French withdrawal to 1862-1874, and the naval officers annexing the remaining Mekong plain. Used for sequence, not inaccessible chapter details.

Original archival guide directly read. It describes the admiral-led government preceding the 1887 union and distinguishes directly administered Cochinchina under a governor from protectorates under residents superior. Its 1862-1954 archive span confirms that 1878 is not the colony end. Institutional catalog directly read. It records a Cochinchina administration course from 1874, Truong Vinh Ky geography of Lower Cochinchina from 1875 and a primary science primer from 1876. Catalog survival proves these books existed, not how many children used them. Institutional essay directly read. It states that the colonial administration published official material from the conquest, including the 1862 Bulletin officiel, and that romanized Vietnamese later expanded authorship and reading. Used to distinguish print technology from the power deciding what was printed.

Early reign dates and borders remain uncertain. Damaged readings remain debated. Archaeologia Adriatica 4 (2010), pp. 53-59, abstract: cemetery by St George above Kastel Sucurac, reidentification of the bronze fitting and late-eighth/early-ninth-century parallels. The object predates the tenth-century royal title evidence. American Journal of Physical Anthropology 148 (2012), pp. 543-556, DOI 10.1002/ajpa.22070; Table 1 and pp. 548-550: adult samples, early medieval millet interpretation and the distinct Sibenik-Sveti Lovre signal. Table A2 dates selected individuals; its dating ranges differ from the broad site labels, so no precise cemetery lifetime is adopted. Starohrvatska prosvjeta III/35 (2008), English abstract and full study pp. 211-238: ninth- to eleventh-century cemetery, skeletal and dental stress, small sample limitations and uncertain hunting interpretation. Skeletal similarity is not used to assign biological ethnicity. 1102 coronation at Biograd recorded in St Mary's Zadar cartulary; royal titles; Zadar's recognition in 1105 and the church inscription. This is dynastic change, not the disappearance of Croatian kingship or society.

Outstanding Universal Value, brief synthesis and criteria(ii)/(iii); sixth to tenth-century cultural scope. No assertion every site inside imported polygon.
John Guy, Making Sense of Dvaravati, printed54 fig7. Exact phrase, translation, findyear/location, date and diameter. No invented Pallava Unicode sequence; preserve diacritics.

Lost Kingdoms printed190, fig119 and adjacent paragraphs. Gravity is scholarly inference and arrangements reconstructed from separate elements; no precise site/date fabricated.
Clay/terracotta plaques paragraphs, seventh to ninth-century subjects and merit generated through stamping. No universal access or imagined workshop owner.
Results fig2/3, Phromtin Tai phase7, and conclusion. Distinguish Dvaravati evidence from much earlier millet sequence and avoid panregional irrigation denial.
Printed49/57 occupation dates; printed63 Other artefacts and fig3. Lamp settings are possibilities; do not infer particular household occupants or gender division.

Modern Indonesian province summary that collides with the medieval regional atlas target. First exact east-java feature, decoded geometry, point ownership, and direct shared-arc audit. Third exact interval, geometry identity with 1100, point ownership, and shared arcs with Srivijaya and malays-1200. Endpoint where east-java disappears and the same tested footprint is assigned to the historically mistimed kediri id. Scholarly volume section checked for late Mataram in East Java, the 1016 attack as remembered by Pucangan, Airlangga's restoration, and subsequent political division. Scope: Used only as broad overview context; its regional reconstruction does not validate the atlas polygon or erase chronological debate. Peer-reviewed synthesis checked for the geographic distinction among Kadiri, Janggala, Singhasari, the upper and lower Brantas, and political continuity. Scope: Used as a broad orientation source, not proof that one state controlled the atlas's multi-island polygon. Peer-reviewed historical framing checked for Kediri as an heir to Airlangga's Kahuripan, its endpoint in 1222, and succession by Singhasari or Tumapel from 1222 to 1292. Scope: Used only for the overview's broad political chronology and the arithmetic of the atlas's 57-year lag; the article's later tiger-ritual argument is outside this card's evidence.

sources.locator: Primary project data were checked locally for exact IDs, names, aliases, date intervals and every historical TopoJSON feature. Cyprus-1960 is distinct from medieval cyprus and modern northern-cyprus; georgia-1994 is distinct from medieval georgia. Point tests and bounds are preserved in this bundle's identity audit. Imported shapes are display data, not legal boundary or effective-control surveys. Primary project GeoJSON was checked locally. The modern file gives Cyprus separate cyprus-1960 and northern-cyprus features but does not reliably excise the British Sovereign Base Areas; the Georgia feature includes tested points at Sukhumi and Tskhinvali. Point tests are aids to disclose geometry, not geopolitical findings.

Met Department of Asian Art essay checked. Ashikaga authority was weaker than Kamakura rule, powerful daimyo retained regional influence, the 1467-1477 Onin War devastated Kyoto, and conflict continued into Sengoku. The period also expanded commercial, transport and urban networks and supported tea, renga, Noh and ink painting.

Sakai City Library reference answer in the NDL cooperative database checked. Yoshitane marched to Kawachi in 1493 and was deposed in a coup led by Hosokawa Masamoto. A rival Ashikaga-Hosokawa-Miyoshi power formed at Sakai in 1527; calling it the “Sakai bakufu” is explicitly identified as one historian’s hypothesis.

Municipal chronology checked. It dates the Onin conflict and fortified Upper and Lower Kyoto, revival of the Gion festival in 1500 after wartime suspension, fighting near Funaokayama in 1511, and expulsion of the last Ashikaga shogun from Kyoto in 1573.

NDL authority record checked. It identifies Ashikaga Yoshiharu (1511-1550), childhood name Kameomaru, as the twelfth shogun of the Muromachi shogunate. The authority record is identity evidence, not a full political biography. Museum detail checked. The screen labels the shogunal residence “くはうさま（公方様）” and identifies it as Yoshiharu’s Yanagihara residence built in 1525. Samurai, visitors and women appear in the compound. The label supplies an authentic short Japanese writing sample. Academic book overview checked. Ming accepted tribute missions, so the shogunate used the title king of Japan for licensed trade. Ship management involved shugo daimyo, temples, shrines and other powers; rivalry between Hosokawa and Ouchi interests led to the 1523 Ningbo incident. The author questions a simple later Ouchi-monopoly story.

sources.locator: Repository index checked for exact id malaya: name Malaya, approximately 1650-1920. Separate records exist for Malacca, Malaysian Islamic states, Brunei and Malaysia, so this card does not merge their identities. Decoded with topojson-client. The exact malaya feature is a two-part MultiPolygon with 178 positions and bbox 100.1404,0.7264 to 119.0442,6.8996. It includes tested Malacca, Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur, Penang and Kota Kinabalu points, but excludes Kota Bharu, Kuala Terengganu, Singapore, Kuching and Bandar Seri Begawan. Official national summary checked for later chronology. The Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957 and joined Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore to form Malaysia in 1963. These later events show why the atlas's 1920 change from malaya to malaysia is anachronistic.

sources.locator: Sections on early Piasts, Boleslaw I coronation in 1025, thirteenth-century fragmentation and Wladyslaw Lokietek coronation in 1320. Later union is checked against its documentary record; apparent typographical errors elsewhere are not adopted. The Early Piasts Residence on Lednica and Archaeological Reserve in Giecz: tenth-century bridges, palace and chapel, unfinished foundations and early-eleventh-century church. Reconstructed homesteads are distinguished from original remains. Brief synthesis: 1257 charter, urban layout, Wawel and separate town of Kazimierz chartered in 1335; Catholic and Jewish communities. Extant buildings are from multiple periods. Opening historical paragraphs: medieval brine production, thirteenth-century exploratory shaft, reconstructed casing, 1290 charter and joint saltworks enterprise. Later mechanisation is not assigned to medieval miners. Foundation and Endowment sections, available through the indexed scholarly project text: royal charter 1364, interruption, renewed charter 1400, endowed chairs in astronomy, mathematics, grammar and rhetoric. The exact operating faculties before 1370 are not asserted. Opening description: July 1569 act as legal foundation of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Constitutional union is distinguished from conquest or disappearance of Polish institutions.

Illustrated nineteenth-century toothbrush is outside this card’s period.

sources.locator: Repository source checked at the frozen bundle revision. The record is id polynesians, name Polynesians, circa 1000-1900, kind culture, generated from historical basemaps. Its alias Beothuk is inconsistent with the name and Pacific geometry and is treated as catalog contamination, not as identity evidence. Indigenous-led institution account checked. It identifies the 1976 voyage, Micronesian master navigator Mau Piailug, a Hawaiian and Pacific crew, use of wind, waves, stars, birds and clouds, and the voyage’s role in renewing Hawaiian voyaging and language commitments. Māori-led national trust history checked. It records the first kōhanga reo at Pukeatua in 1982, whānau governance, immersion in te reo Māori and intergenerational community action. Used as one specific continuity example, not as a proxy for all Polynesian language movements.

Tonga National Commission for UNESCO submission checked. It reports more than 30 Tongan Lapita sites, initial settlement around 2,800 years ago, beach and small-island locations, decorated and plain pottery, shell and stone artifacts, faunal remains, transported food resources, and ongoing debate about ultimate origins. Peer-reviewed open article checked. Its screened short-lived samples support Society Islands settlement about 1025-1120 and a later major pulse about 1190-1290. The authors call the model falsifiable and explain why older charcoal and marine samples can produce misleadingly early dates. Decoded with topojson-client. The polynesians feature for 1000-1100 is a three-part MultiPolygon with 48 positions and bbox -158.46458464584646,18.94575359308675 to -154.91854918549186,21.689646959512046. The three parts are Hawaiʻi, Oʻahu and Maui, not a boundary around Polynesia.

Tonga National Commission submission checked. It describes Heketā and Lapaha, monumental stone structures, about 22 royal tomb platforms, and Lapaha as a chiefly centre of a Tongan maritime chiefdom from the thirteenth to nineteenth centuries. Living burial traditions are also noted. World Heritage entry checked. The Raʻiātea cultural landscape includes valleys, lagoon, reef and ocean; its marae was political, ceremonial and funerary. UNESCO describes an alliance linked by chiefly gatherings and voyaging, not a single government ruling all Polynesian peoples. Official park page checked. It defines aiga as extended family, matai leadership as service, village fono as councils of family titleholders, communal land, shared work and resources, respect for elders, and living faʻasamoa. These Samoan patterns are not generalized to every Polynesian society. New Zealand national encyclopedia page checked for whānau, hapū and iwi relationships, rangatira leadership, mana and tapu, regional authority and exchange. It does not describe one Māori state, still less one pan-Polynesian state.

Official historical narrative checked. It distinguishes Kamehameha control of Hawaiʻi Island, conquest of Maui, Lānaʻi, Molokaʻi and Oʻahu by 1795, and Kauaʻi paramount chief Kaumualiʻi acknowledging supremacy in 1810, completing the consolidation of the Hawaiian Kingdom. State cultural narrative checked, especially Population Loss Caused by Disease. It attributes severe post-1778 Native Hawaiian population decline to introduced infections and explains resulting loss of people, homes, gardens, fishponds, stories and practices. Exact pre-contact population estimates remain debated and are omitted.

Minute coordinate drift begins the 1400 to 1492 interval without a meaningful territorial shift. The exact id disappears for eight years and shuar-wampis owns the audited core and Gualaquiza. The target returns with its former component for 1500 to 1530 while Inca owns audited western points. A minimally shifted seven-point component covers 1530 to 1600. The same target component continues for 1600 to 1650. The target persists for 1650 to 1700 while outside audited points are assigned to the Viceroyalty of Peru. Another hash change without meaningful extent change begins 1700 to 1715. Target coverage continues while the atlas changes surrounding ownership from Peru to Spain. Minute geometry drift begins the 1783 to 1800 interval. The component persists from 1800 to 1815 with a changed geometry hash. Last exact interval, 1815 to 1878; seven audited core points remain target-owned. Target vanishes as Ecuador and Peru replace Indigenous layers at audited points.

sources.locator: The Crown established a viceroyalty in 1535 after the 1521 conquest; Indigenous communities faced epidemics, coerced labor and imposed institutions but persisted. In 1535 the viceroyalty governed Mexico, Guatemala, the Caribbean, Florida and southwestern North America from Mexico City. Colonial legal records cover New Spain and later Mexican states, with historical jurisdiction extending well beyond modern Mexico. Sixteenth-century epidemic diseases devastated Native communities and disrupted their societies. In 1571 Indigenous Nahuatl officials used a pictorial legal record to complain of mistreatment and underpayment. Nahua students wrote Nahuatl in Latin letters and painted illustrations; a Spanish translation stands beside their text. Silver left New Spain for Asian goods; silk and porcelain came to Acapulco and influenced Mexican arts. Viceroy regulated public baths and temazcales, including women’s and men’s facilities and permanent Spanish signs. Museum displays a pharmacy, infirmary garden, kitchen, refectory, convent women and the diverse late-colonial Mexico City plaza.
